summary: Archives the report of the joint IETF and ITU-T working team on applying MPLS to transport networks. The team recommended that the two organizations work together, bringing transport requirements into the IETF and extending MPLS forwarding, OAM, survivability, network management, and control plane protocols to meet them. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5317 archives the report of a joint team of the IETF and the ITU-T that looked at how to extend MPLS so it could carry transport networks. The team recommended that the two organizations work together rather than build incompatible versions of the same technology, and that the result be called the MPLS Transport Profile.

questions: why did ietf and itu-t work together on mpls
what did the joint working team recommend
subtitle: The agreement that stopped two standards bodies from building incompatible versions of the same thing.

tldr.problem: The ITU-T was building a connection-oriented packet technology for transport networks, T-MPLS, based on IETF MPLS but not compatible with it, and the IETF warned that two incompatible versions would be a danger to both the Internet and the transport network.
tldr.mechanism: A joint team of both organizations reviewed the work in five areas, forwarding, OAM, protection, the control plane and network management, and looked for obstacles to making T-MPLS a profile of IETF MPLS.
tldr.outcome: The team found no show stoppers and recommended that the two work together, producing the MPLS Transport Profile, MPLS-TP. ITU-T management accepted the recommendation.

facts.label: Work groups the review was split into

today: RFC 5317 is an Informational document that archives a report, and it is not listed as obsoleted or updated. The ITU-T accepted the JWT recommendations, as recorded in the May 2008 liaison statement, and the IETF work that followed produced the MPLS Transport Profile.

sections.title: Introduction and Background
sections.content:
For a number of years the ITU-T had been designing a connection-oriented packet switched technology for use in transport networks. A transport network is the network that provides wide area connectivity on which other services, such as IP or the phone network, run. The ITU-T chose to adapt the IETF's MPLS to the task and introduced a protocol suite known as T-MPLS.

Quite late in the ITU-T design and specification cycle there were a number of liaison exchanges between the two organizations, and the chairs of the MPLS, PWE3, BFD and CCAMP working groups, along with the Routing and Internet Area Directors, attended several ITU-T meetings. Through this process the IETF became increasingly concerned that the incompatibility of IETF MPLS and ITU-T T-MPLS would represent a mutual danger to both the Internet and the transport network. Those concerns led the chairs of the IESG and IAB to send a liaison to the ITU-T stating that either T-MPLS should become fully compliant MPLS, standardized under the IETF process, the so-called Option 1, or it should become a completely disjoint protocol with a new name and completely new set of code points, the so-called Option 2.

Both options were discussed at an ITU-T meeting of Question 12 of Study Group 15 in Stuttgart, where it was proposed that a joint team should be formed to evaluate the issues and make a recommendation to ITU-T management on the best way forward. Following discussion between the management of the two organizations, a Joint Working Team was established, supported by an IETF Design Team and an Ad Hoc Group on T-MPLS in the ITU-T. The first meeting of the Ad Hoc group occurred during the ITU-T Geneva Plenary in February 2008. As a result of the work of the JWT and the agreement on a way forward, the fears that a set of next-generation network transport specifications developed by the ITU-T could cause interoperability problems were allayed.

The JWT submitted its report to the ITU-T and IETF management in the form of a set of PowerPoint slides. The ITU-T accepted the JWT recommendations, as documented in the liaison statement of May 2008. This RFC archives the report in a format accessible to the IETF: an ASCII version holding a summary of the slides, and a PDF version holding the summary and a copy of the slides. In the case of a conflict between the summary and the slides, the slides take precedence.

The starting point of the analysis was to try to satisfy Option 1 by showing the high-level architecture, any show stoppers, and the design points that would need addressing after the decision to work together. Option 1 was stated as preferred by the IETF, and because it was shown to be feasible, Option 2 was not explored. The work was segmented into five groups looking at forwarding, OAM, protection, the control plane, and network management.
sections.plainLanguage: Transport networks carry things like telephone calls and IP traffic over wide areas. The ITU-T wanted to build its transport version of MPLS, but it was drifting away from the version the IETF had standardized, so the two organizations were heading towards a future with two incompatible label-switching systems on the same network. A joint team was set up to decide what to do.

sections.title: Executive Summary: The Recommendation
sections.content:
The JWT achieved consensus on recommending Option 1: to jointly agree to work together, bring transport requirements into the IETF, and extend IETF MPLS forwarding, OAM, survivability, network management and control plane protocols to meet those requirements through the IETF Standards Process. The team believed this would fulfil the mutual goals of improving the functionality of the transport networks and the Internet, and of guaranteeing complete interoperability and architectural soundness. This technology would be referred to as the Transport Profile for MPLS, MPLS-TP.

Future work should focus on defining the MPLS Transport Profile in the IETF, and in the ITU-T on integrating MPLS-TP into the transport network, aligning the current T-MPLS Recommendations with MPLS-TP, and terminating the work on current T-MPLS. The technical feasibility analysis concluded there were no show stopper issues in the Option 1 recommendation, and that the IETF MPLS and Pseudowire architecture could be extended to support transport functional requirements, so there was no need to analyse any other option.

The JWT recommended that the normative definition of MPLS-TP supporting the ITU-T transport network requirements be captured in IETF RFCs, and proposed that the ITU-T should develop Recommendations allowing MPLS-TP to be integrated with current transport equipment and networks, including, in agreement with the IETF, the definition of any ITU-T-specific functionality within the MPLS-TP architecture via the MPLS change process, revise existing Recommendations to align with MPLS-TP, and make normative references to the appropriate RFCs.

The JWT also proposed that the MPLS Interoperability Design Team, the JWT and the Ad Hoc T-MPLS groups continue, with the roles of facilitating the rapid exchange of information between the IETF and ITU-T, ensuring that the work progresses with a consistent set of priorities, identifying gaps and inconsistencies in the solutions under development, proposing solutions for consideration by the appropriate working group or question, and providing guidance when work is stalled or a technical decision must be mediated. None of these groups would have the authority to create or modify IETF RFCs or ITU-T Recommendations; any such work would go through the normal process of the respective standards body, with direct participation by experts from both.

In its conclusion the JWT found no show stoppers and unanimously agreed that it had identified a viable solution. It stated that in its view the existing MPLS architecture can be extended to meet the requirements of a transport profile, and that the architecture allows for a single OAM technology for label switched paths, pseudowires and a deeply nested network. From probing the ITU-T Study Groups and IETF Working Groups it appeared that the MPLS reserved label 14 had had wide enough implementation and deployment that the solution might have to use a different reserved label, for example label 13. The JWT recommended that extensions to label 14 should cease, and further recommended that this architecture appeared to subsume Y.1711, since the requirements can be met by the mechanism proposed in the report.
sections.plainLanguage: The answer was to stop writing two protocols. The transport requirements would be brought into the IETF, and the existing MPLS protocols would be extended to cover them, with the result called the MPLS Transport Profile. The team found nothing that made this impossible, and it also asked that work on extending the old reserved label stop, since that label had been implemented widely enough to cause trouble.

sections.title: High-Level Architecture
sections.content:
Slides 23 to 28 of the report give a high-level architectural view of the proposed design. They describe the spectrum of services the MPLS-TP needs to address and the wider MPLS context, together with the provisioning issues. They also define some basic terminology needed to understand MPLS-TP and give context examples.

The detailed sections of the report then work through the technical areas. The OAM and forwarding slides describe the OAM requirements and discuss segment recovery and node identification, then introduce the OAM hierarchy and describe label switched path monitoring, the relationship between the Maintenance End Point and the Maintenance Intermediate Point, and the relationship between LSP and pseudowire monitoring. Later slides introduce the Associated Channel Header and its generalization to carry OAM over LSPs through the use of the Label for You. A further set of slides describes in detail how forwarding and the Associated Channel Header OAM mechanism work, walking through a significant number of scenarios case by case, and introduces a new textual notation to simplify the description of complex MPLS stacks. The report notes that MPLS forwarding, as specified by the IETF RFCs, requires no changes to support MPLS-TP.
sections.plainLanguage: The architecture slides set out the services the profile has to cover and the terms used to describe it. The technical detail follows in five areas, and the first of them is the one that matters most for carrying traffic: the forwarding plane itself needs no change at all, only the operations and maintenance around it.

sections.title: Control Plane, Survivability and Network Management
sections.content:
The control plane sub-team stated that existing IETF protocols can provide the functions required for transport network operation and for data-communications-network and switched-circuit-network operation. IETF GMPLS protocols have already been applied to the Automatic Switched Optical Network architecture, and the JWT considered that any protocol extensions needed would be easy to make. The slides give a number of scenarios to demonstrate that conclusion.

The survivability sub-team did not find any issues that prevented the creation of an MPLS-TP, and therefore recommended that Option 1 be selected. It identified three potential solutions, each with different attributes and advantages, and thought that further work in the design phase should eliminate one or more of the options or provide an applicability statement. After some clarifications and discussion, the slide set follows with a number of linear and ring protection scenarios with examples of how they might be addressed.

The network management sub-team reached the same conclusion: it found no issues that prevent the creation of an MPLS-TP, and hence Option 1 could be selected.
sections.plainLanguage: The remaining three areas all came back clear. The existing control plane protocols were already good enough, the protection and restoration options could be narrowed down later, and network management raised no obstacle. Nothing in these areas stopped the two organizations from working together.

sections.title: IANA and Security Considerations
sections.content:
No IANA considerations arise from this document. Any allocations needed to implement the JWT recommendation will be requested in the Standards-Track RFCs that define the MPLS-TP protocol.

The only security consideration that arises from this document is the need to ensure that it is a faithful representation of the JWT report. The protocol work that arises from the agreement will have technical security requirements that will be identified in the RFCs that define MPLS-TP.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing to allocate and nothing to secure yet. The only requirement here is that the archived report stays faithful to what the team actually decided, and the real security work belongs to the specifications that follow.

viz.caption: THE TWO OPTIONS THE IESG AND IAB PUT TO THE ITU-T

cells: T-MPLS becomes fully compliant MPLS, standardized under the IETF process
Chosen. The two organizations work together and the result is the MPLS Transport Profile
T-MPLS becomes a completely disjoint protocol with a new name and completely new set of code points
Not explored, because Option 1 was shown to be feasible

viz.caption: THE FIVE AREAS THE REVIEW WAS SPLIT INTO AND WHAT EACH FOUND

items.title: Forwarding
items.text: MPLS forwarding as specified by the IETF RFCs needs no changes to support MPLS-TP.

items.title: OAM
items.text: Requirements for operations, administration and management, with a hierarchy over LSPs and pseudowires and the Associated Channel Header.

items.title: Protection
items.text: No issue preventing an MPLS-TP. Three candidate solutions, to be narrowed down later, with linear and ring scenarios.

items.title: Control plane
items.text: Existing IETF protocols already provide the needed functions; GMPLS has been applied to ASON, and any extensions would be easy.

items.title: Network management
items.text: No issue preventing an MPLS-TP, so Option 1 could be selected.
